title: The Docket — spot the flaws (your Property Law material)

items.text: The transfer of ownership of goods is generally governed by the principle of delivery alone, regardless of the parties' agreement.
items.ground: This principle is central to the discussion in Sagaert's article, which contrasts consensual systems with delivery systems in European private law.
items.cite: V. Sagaert, Consensual versus Delivery Systems in European Private Law – Consensus about Tradition? In: Rules for the Transfer of Movables. A Candidate for European Harmonisation or National Reforms?, W. Faber & B. Lurger, eds., Munich 2008, pp. 9-46
items.why: Sagaert's analysis emphasizes that consensual systems require agreement between parties for the transfer of ownership, in contrast to systems where delivery alone suffices.

items.text: The transfer of ownership of goods is generally governed by the principle of consensual transfer, which requires a meeting of minds between the parties regarding the transfer of ownership.
items.ground: This principle is central to the discussion in Sagaert's article, which contrasts consensual systems with delivery systems in European private law.
items.cite: V. Sagaert, Consensual versus Delivery Systems in European Private Law – Consensus about Tradition? In: Rules for the Transfer of Movables. A Candidate for European Harmonisation or National Reforms?, W. Faber & B. Lurger, eds., Munich 2008, pp. 9-46
items.why: Sagaert's analysis emphasizes that consensual systems require agreement between parties for the transfer of ownership, in contrast to systems where delivery alone suffices.

items.text: Acquisitive prescription does not allow for the acquisition of ownership of goods; it only serves to protect possession of immovable property.
items.ground: This principle is discussed in the context of the DCFR and is analyzed by Salomons, who evaluates how acquisitive prescription fits into the broader framework of property law.
items.cite: A.F. Salomons, The Purpose and Coherence of the Rules on Good Faith Acquisition and Acquisitive Prescription in the Draft Common Frame of Reference: A Tale of Two Gatekeepers, ERPL 2013-3, p. 843-862
items.why: Salomons explores how acquisitive prescription functions as a legal mechanism for acquiring ownership, similar to good faith acquisition, within the DCFR.

items.text: Acquisitive prescription allows a person to acquire ownership of goods after a certain period of continuous and peaceful possession, provided they meet the conditions set out in the relevant legal system.
items.ground: This principle is discussed in the context of the DCFR and is analyzed by Salomons, who evaluates how acquisitive prescription fits into the broader framework of property law.
items.cite: A.F. Salomons, The Purpose and Coherence of the Rules on Good Faith Acquisition and Acquisitive Prescription in the Draft Common Frame of Reference: A Tale of Two Gatekeepers, ERPL 2013-3, p. 843-862
items.why: Salomons explores how acquisitive prescription functions as a legal mechanism for acquiring ownership, similar to good faith acquisition, within the DCFR.

items.text: Limited rights can be acquired through the same mechanisms as full ownership, such as purchase or inheritance.
items.ground: The introduction by F.M.J. Verstijlen discusses how limited rights are created through particular legal instruments.
items.cite: F.M.J. Verstijlen - Introduction to limited rights
items.why: The author explains that limited rights require specific legal creation mechanisms as opposed to general ownership acquisition.

items.text: Limited rights in property law are typically acquired through specific legal mechanisms rather than general acquisition rules.
items.ground: The introduction by F.M.J. Verstijlen discusses how limited rights are created through particular legal instruments.
items.cite: F.M.J. Verstijlen - Introduction to limited rights
items.why: The author explains that limited rights require specific legal creation mechanisms as opposed to general ownership acquisition.
